Brain 18F-FDG-PET characteristics in patients with
paraneoplastic neurological syndrome and its correlation with
clinical and MRI findings
Neil Masangkay a, Sandip Basu a,b, Mateen Moghbel a, Thomas Kwee c and
Abass Alavi a
Aim This study aimed to examine the imaging
characteristics and clinical and MRI correlates of brain
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18F-FDG)-PET imaging in patients
with paraneoplatic neurological syndrome.
Materials and methods Data of patients diagnosed with
paraneoplastic neurological syndrome were retrospectively
reviewed using the electronic medical records of the
patients, looking specifically at records of hospital stays,
laboratory findings and imaging reports. Both brain MRI and
18F-FDG-PET imaging characteristics were analyzed and
compared.
Results A total of 19 patients (ages 26 –78; 13 female and
six male patients) with clinical diagnoses of PNS were
analyzed in this study. Limbic encephalitis (paraneoplastic
limbic encephalitis) was found in 10 patients, seven of
whom had a diagnosis of cancer. Brain 18F-FDG-PET
showed bilaterally increased mesial temporal 18F-FDG
uptake in eight of 10 patients with limbic encephalitis;
seven of these eight patients exhibited memory loss. There
was also a notable reduction in general cortical 18F-FDG
uptake (including in the primary visual cortex) in six of the
10 patients with limbic encephalitis; three of the six patients
had their primary motor cortices spared, two of them being
spared bilaterally. Five of the seven limbic encephalitis
patients with diagnosed cancer and two of the three without
it had the aforementioned cortical and temporal lobe
findings. Of the eight patients with onconeuronal antibodies,
seven had temporal lobe enhancement and a total of six
had diffuse cortical dysfunction. One patient with
paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis without antibodies had
demonstrated severely increased 18F-FDG uptake in both
occipital lobes extending to the temporal lobes. The other
patient without antibodies had a normal PET scan. Only one
patient among four with paraneoplastic cerebellar
degeneration had demonstrated decreased cerebellar
uptake on 18F-FDG-PET that correlated with atrophy of the
cerebellar vermis on MRI. Three patients had a clinical
diagnosis of sensory neuropathy, of whom one
demonstrated mild bilateral decrease in 18F-FDG uptake in
the mesial temporal lobes, one showed notable increase in
18F-FDG uptake in the right mesial temporal lobe (with
normal MRI) and the other had a normal brain 18F-FDG-PET.
One patient was found to have cerebellar findings paired
with oculomotor findings and showed increased
18F-FDG
uptake in the cerebellum. One patient with stiff-person
syndrome had normal brain 18F-FDG-PET.
Conclusion The pattern of abnormalities in the brain
18F-FDG-PET images usually correlates well with the
corresponding clinical settings and presentations. Although
quite frequently findings correlate with those of MRI, at
times 18F-FDG-PET can demonstrate functional abnormality
in the absence of any MRI finding, which could give a
therapeutic window before anatomical changes set in. Nucl

Introduction
Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNS) are a group
of rare central nervous system disorders that are triggered
by an immune system response to a neoplasm. The
classical neurological syndromes in PNS include ence-
phalomyelitis, limbic encephalitis, cerebellar degenera-
tion, opsoclonus–myoclonus, and sensory neuropathy [1].
Most cases of PNS are accompanied by onconeuronal
antibodies. Of these, some antibodies, such as anti-Hu,
anti-Yo, anti-CV2, anti-Ri, anti-Ma2, and anti-
amphiphysin, are better understood and are thus classi-
fied as ‘well-characterized’ [1]. In addition to these
antibodies, there are also several partially characterized
onconeuronal antibodies. In about two-thirds of cases
with an antineuronal antibody, the neurological symp-
toms precede the diagnosis of a tumor by up to 4 years

[2]. The treatment of the underlying malignancy, when it
can be detected, is considered the optimal treatment
for PNS.
The applications of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18F-FDG)-
PET in PNS are evolving, with an increasing number of
reports emphasizing the potential of this modality in the
understanding and diagnosis of PNS [1]. The role of
18F-FDG-PET in PNS encompasses two major applica-
tions: (a) assessment of the functional neurologic con-
sequences of the disease in the brain as well as their
clinical correlates and changes that follow after ther-
apeutic interventions; and (b) detection of occult malig-
nant foci. In this study, we examined the clinical utility of
brain 18F-FDG-PET imaging in paraneoplatic neurolo-
gical syndrome from the aforementioned perspective.
Materials and methods
Patient population
We reviewed the brain 18F-FDG-PET studies of 19
patients (ages 26 –78 years, 13 female) with clinical
diagnoses of PNS. All patients were evaluated at the
Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania and under-
went brain PET scans at the same center for the eva-
luation of brain
18F-FDG-PET characteristics and their
clinical correlates.
We conducted retrospective data reviews of the 19
patients using the electronic medical records of the
patients analyzed, looking specifically at records of hos-
pital stays, laboratory findings, and imaging reports.
Patients also had their cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) exam-
ined for the presence of antibodies within their sera. Of
the 19 patients, 10 had paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis
(PLE), four had cerebellar degeneration, three had sen-
sory neuropathy, one had a combination of ocular and
cerebellar findings, and one had stiff-person syndrome.
All brain PET scans as well as brain MRI scans were
completed at the Hospital of the University of
Pennsylvania and read by a staff radiologist. While
studying MRI findings, we looked for written imaging
reports. For studying PET scans, we conducted a retro-
spective review of the actual PET images of the patients.
Results
Limbic encephalitis
Limbic encephalitis was diagnosed in 10 patients, seven
of whom were diagnosed with cancer. Out of this subset
of patients with limbic encephalitis, all but two were
found to have onconeuronal antibodies in their CSF (two
patients with anti-Hu antibodies, two with antineuronal
cell membrane antibodies, two with anti-voltage-gated
K-channel antibodies, one with anti-NMDR, and one
with an ‘atypical’ antibody) (Tables 1 and 2).
PET studies showed bilaterally increased mesial tem-
poral
18F-FDG uptake in eight of the 10 patients with
limbic encephalitis (with no significant trend in later-
ality), and of these eight patients seven exhibited
memory loss. There was also a notable reduction in
general cortical
18F-FDG uptake (including in the pri-
mary visual cortex) in six of the 10 patients with limbic
encephalitis. Three of these six patients had their pri-
mary motor cortices spared, with two of them being
spared bilaterally. An example is illustrated in Figs 1
and 2.
As noted above, cancer was found in seven patients. Five
of the seven limbic encephalitis patients with cancer and
two of the three without it had the aforementioned cor-
tical and temporal lobe findings. Of the eight patients
with onconeuronal antibodies, seven had temporal lobe
enhancement and six had diffuse cortical dysfunction.
One patient without antibodies had PET showing
severely increased
18F-FDG uptake in both occipital

lobes extending to the temporal lobes. The other patient
without antibodies had a normal PET scan (completed a
year after the initial presentation of symptoms).
All of the patients in this study with limbic encephalitis
had also undergone brain MRI. Of these 10 patients,
eight had temporal lobe involvement in one or more of
their MRI studies. Seven of these patients also had
bilateral temporal lobe involvement in their brain PET
scans. One patient with temporal lobe abnormalities on
MRI had a normal PET (Table 2, patient 6), whereas one
patient with temporal lobe abnormalities noted on PET
had only cortical and cerebellar involvement on MRI
(Table 2, patient 5).

Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
Four of the 19 patients were clinically diagnosed with
cerebellar degeneration. All four patients had a current or
prior history of a tumor [two with small cell lung cancer
(SCLC) and two with breast cancer], and one patient had
bilateral breast cancer preceding her evaluation for cer-
ebellar symptoms. From an immunological standpoint,
only one of these patients had a well-characterized
onconeuronal antibody (anti-Yo). One other patient had
an ‘atypical’ antibody found in the sera, whereas two
others had no antibodies at all (Table 3).
Of these four, only one patient had any significant PET
findings (Table 3, patient 1). This patient was found to
have a decrease in cerebellar uptake on
18F-FDG-PET
scans (Fig. 3), which correlated with atrophy of the
cerebellar vermis on MRI studies from May 2002 to
May 2004. Other PET scans did not show any particular
pattern of signal loss, or were normal.
Sensory neuropathy
Clinical sensory neuropathy was found in three patients,
all of whom had a malignancy (one with Hurthle cell
thyroid cancer and two with SCLC). Both patients with
SCLC were found to have anti-Hu antibodies, while the
third patient did not have any antibodies in her CSF.
The patient with Hurthle cell thyroid cancer was found
to have mild bilateral decrease in the uptake of 18F-FDG
in the mesial temporal lobes. Her 18F-FDG-PET scan

was also notable for a mild generalized decrease in

of the primary motor cortices. One patient with SCLC
had normal brain 18F-FDG-PET. A second patient with
SCLC was found to have only a notable increase in
18F-FDG uptake in the right mesial temporal lobe over
two different scans. She was subsequently treated and
showed clinical improvement. Follow-up PET scans did
not show progression of her temporal lobe lesion on her
left side, and MRI was normal (Table 4).
Oculomotor findings
One patient was found to have cerebellar findings paired
with oculomotor findings. He was subsequently found to
have a metastatic carcinoma in addition to anti-Ri anti-
bodies. This patient ’s PET scan was noted for increased
18F-FDG uptake in his cerebellum as well as some
findings of right-sided encephalomalacia, presumably
from a previous injury. He had not undergone an MRI
(Table 5).
Stiff-person syndrome
One patient was found to have stiff-person syndrome
with anti-GAD antibodies. This patient was not found to
have cancer and her PET scan was deemed normal
(Table 6).
Discussion
In PNS, conventional anatomic imaging modalities are
often unable to identify a primary causative tumor.
Hence, the majority of existing research studies with
18F-FDG-PET [1–5] have focused their objectives in this
particular domain. Brain 18F-FDG-PET findings have
been explored by a handful of reports where the PET
imaging results have been compared with the clinical
presentation. In the study by Ances et al. [6], who studied
the value of brain MRI and 18F-FDG-PET in seven
patients with subacute limbic encephalitis who had
abnormal CSF (six had pleocytosis, six had increased
protein concentration, and three had oligoclonal bands),
all but one patient showed 18F-FDG hypermetabolism in
one or both temporal lobes on PET. In four patients with
predominant hippocampal dysfunction, MRI abnormal-
ities were restricted to one or both medial temporal lobes.
One patient had additional hyperactivity in the brainstem
and hypoactivity in the occipital lobes, whereas two other
patients had additional sites of abnormal activity in the
cerebellum. Overall, the authors concluded that PET and
MRI complemented each other but did not overlap in
50% of the patients. Scheid et al. [7] performed serial
MRI and
18F-FDG-PET in a single patient with anti-
Ma2-positive PLE. They observed increasing focal
hypermetabolism on 18F-FDG-PET in the left medial
temporal lobe (among four consecutive PET scans) along
with stable MRI findings. This hypermetabolism was
associated with an increase in the western blot serum
anti-Ma2 antibody titers [7]. A critical review of the

literature by these authors [7] revealed pronounced dis-
crepancies between MRI and PET findings. Many of the
previous investigators concluded that the focal hyper-
metabolism on PET may represent seizure activity [8,9],
whereas others considered the PET abnormalities as
representing an underlying inflammatory process [10
–12]. Overall, it can be concluded from these studies that
18F-FDG-PET usually shows hypermetabolism in one or
both temporal lobes in patients with PLE. In para-
neoplastic cerebellar degeneration, brain PET studies
generally revealed decreased 18F-FDG activity in the
cerebellum, whereas brain MRI studies showed cere-
bellar atrophy, often in the later stages of the disease. At
times, both studies may appear normal in the early stages
of the disease, though 18F-FDG-PET tends to show
abnormality more often compared with MRI [13]. There
are two reported exceptions [14,15] in the literature with
regard to the above-mentioned facts. Choi et al. [14]
reported a solitary case in which cerebellar
18F-FDG
hypermetabolism was observed rather than hypometa-
bolism. This, they concluded, was due to an acute
inflammatory process associated with an immunological
reaction [14]. Scheid et al. [15] reported a patient in whom
cerebellar atrophy was documented by MRI very early in
the disease course. So far, the literature does not contain
descriptions of typical brain features in other types of
PNS, such as opsoclonus –myoclonus or subacute sensory
neuronopathy. More data need to be collected through
carefully conducted studies [16].
As noted from the above-mentioned results of our study,
brain PET scans in limbic encephalitis have shown a
tendency for a bilateral increase in mesial temporal lobe
18F-FDG uptake in eight of 10 study patients, with seven
of these eight having experienced memory difficulty. In
addition, we have noted occasional decreases in general
cortical
18F-FDG uptake, with regions surrounding the
central sulcus being spared. With respect to the corre-
sponding MRI studies for patients with limbic
encephalitis, most of the brain PET studies with tem-
poral lobe findings correlated with T2 and/or fluid atte-
nuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities on
MRI. The presence of increased temporal
18F-FDG
uptake in the presence of symptoms such as memory loss
and confusion could suggest inflammation as the cause of
these imaging findings. The reduced
18F-FDG uptake
observed in the cortices of these patients could be attri-
butable to generalized hypoactivity caused by para-
neoplastic syndromes or even sedatives given to the
patients.
In patients with cerebellar degeneration, only one of four
with clinical cerebellar symptoms had significant findings
on PET. This patient ’s
18F-FDG-PET study (Table 3,
patient 1) showed a severe decrease in 18F-FDG uptake
in the cerebellum. The MRI also showed mild atrophy of
the cerebellar vermis a few months before her PET scan
was completed. This patient was also the only patient out
of this group with a well-characterized antibody in her
CSF (anti-Yo). It can be assumed that this patient ’s
findings are due to extensive cerebellar tissue damage
being manifested as atrophy on MRI and a lack of
18F-FDG uptake on PET (and henceforth a lack of cel-
lular activity). Of the other three patients, one was a
63-year-old man with SCLC, no discernible pattern on
PET, and an MRI with findings only consistent with
small-vessel ischemia. The other two patients also had a

history of cancer and clinical cerebellar symptoms, but
normal PET studies. Looking closely at these three, one
should note that none of them had well-characterized
antibodies, nor did they have any MRI findings that were
notable for any cerebellar dysfunction. The lack of
findings may mean that these patients ’ syndromes were
too early in their course or not severe enough at the time
of imaging to show any significant findings. In this study,
we noted a single patient with oculomotor symptoms
along with cerebellar dysfunction and anti-Ri antibodies,
but no tumor. His PET study showed increased uptake

of 18F-FDG in the cerebellum. As there was only a single
patient with this condition, it is difficult to properly arrive
at a conclusion regarding the relationship between the
patient’s physical symptoms and the imaging findings.
Of the three patients with sensory neuropathy who were
studied in the present series, two had significant PET
findings. One patient (Table 4, patient 1) had a mild
increase in 18F-FDG uptake in both temporal lobes along
with a mild decrease in cortical 18F-FDG uptake, fol-
lowing a pattern that was seen in many of the patients
with limbic encephalitis. Another patient also had
increased mesial temporal lobe uptake but this finding
was only unilateral (Table 4, patient 2). This patient
underwent two separate PET scans completed 2 months
apart, both with right-sided temporal lobe findings.
Clinically, this patient experienced several symptoms,
including numbness, gait difficulty, and weakness, but
never had the full cascade of symptoms associated
with limbic encephalitis (confusion, memory difficulty,
decreased level of consciousness) and his condition
improved after treatment.
One of the shortcomings of this study as it currently
stands is that the number of patients is small, an inherent
difficulty posed by a rare set of syndromes such as PNS.
Clearly, more statistical power would be needed to con-
firm the presence or absence of any particular pattern of
18F-FDG uptake in these disorders. Larger studies are
required to examine the brain PET findings in para-
neoplastic syndromes.
